text.text: Run every commission from one page: clients, projects by design phase, the drawing sets due, RFIs and submittals waiting on the office, and hours against budget. Open the Dashboard on Monday, check Days to permit submission on every project, and clear the RFIs older than a week first.

This workspace runs the office of a small architecture practice: clients and projects by phase, fees and hours against budget, the drawing sets you issue, and the RFIs and submittals that arrive once construction starts. Drawings stay in your design software; this is where the practice sees what is due, what is waiting and whether each fee is holding.

text.text: Architectural work moves through standard phases. Each one ends with a client decision, and a phase is only finished when its exit check is done. That protects the schedule and the fee.

cells.text: RFIs, submittals, site visits, pay applications

text.text: When the exit check is met, get the client's sign-off in writing.
Move the project to the next phase and bill the fee for the phase just finished.

A change after a sign-off is extra work. Write it down, estimate hours, and agree an additional fee before the drawings change. Small changes add up; a running list kept on the project keeps the conversation calm.
Check construction cost at the end of schematic design and design development. If the scheme is over budget, adjust now; redesign during construction documents is the most expensive kind.

Greenmount Lofts Building B is in design development with the steel shop drawings already coming in for review. The team issues the design development set this week and asks the developer for written sign-off before construction documents start.
. Respond to building department comments within a week; slow responses are the most common cause of permitting delays.
Bring structural, mechanical and electrical consultants in by design development at the latest. Coordination problems found on paper cost hours; the same problems found on site cost the client money.
At hand-over, issue as-built drawings, warranties and the close-out binder, then set the project to
During construction, the contractor's questions and product submissions come to the architect. Fast, clear answers keep the job moving; slow ones become delay claims.
Log each RFI the day it arrives with the question, who asked it, and the date an answer is due (usually five working days).
if it could. Those go to the project architect and the client immediately.
Answer with a sketch or a reference to the drawings, not just words.

text.text: Check each submittal against the specification section and drawings. Stamp it, write comments clearly, and return it by the review due date.
RFIs and submittals due in two days assigned to a person
Anything overdue answered today, or the contractor told when
Cost or schedule items raised with the client
Structural, mechanical and electrical items go to the right consultant the same day. Track their reply date too; their delay is still your delay.
Answer the question asked, and only that.
Refer to sheet and detail numbers.
If the answer changes the drawings, issue a revised sheet.

The bakery's exhaust hood submittal was due back three days ago. The architect reviews it this morning, approves with comments on clearances, and calls the kitchen supplier so the order is not held up.
Every RFI and submittal stays in the workspace with its dates. If a dispute comes up later, this record shows what was asked, when, and what you answered.
Many RFIs on one detail usually mean the drawing is unclear. Fix the drawing for the next project.
Architecture fees are earned by the hour, even when billed as a fixed fee. Tracking hours by phase shows early when a project is losing money.
Everyone logs time daily: project, phase, hours and a short description.

The Elmwood fit-out is 85 percent billed and in construction administration, but hours are close to budget. The partner checks the RFI log, finds most hours went on the oven pad and duct conflict, and raises an additional services fee for the extra site visits.
Time logged but not yet billed is money the practice has earned and not collected. Review it monthly, and bill hourly work the month it happens.
Use logged hours from past projects of the same kind to price the next one. Real numbers beat guesses every time.
Site visits during construction let the architect see whether the work follows the drawings. A short, consistent routine and a written report after each visit protect the client and the practice.
Latest drawings, open RFIs and submittals on your tablet
Last visit's report and its open items
Hard hat, boots, high-visibility vest and eye protection
Contractor told the time; site supervisor available
Sign in and follow the site safety rules.
Walk the whole site with the supervisor, starting with last visit's open items.
Compare the work with the drawings: dimensions, materials, details.
Photograph each issue with a reference: grid line, room or detail number.
Note anything that needs an RFI answer or a revised drawing.

text.text: Write a short report within two days: date, who was there, progress, issues with photos, and actions with owners and dates.
Add any new questions as RFIs.
Log the visit time against the project in construction administration.
The architect observes and reports; the contractor directs the work and is responsible for site safety. Do not instruct workers directly; raise issues with the supervisor.

At the bakery fit-out, the duct run still clashes with the beam at gridline C. The architect photographs it, adds it to the report, and follows up on the open RFI with the mechanical engineer the same afternoon.
Agree the number of visits in the fee proposal, such as every two weeks during construction. Extra visits caused by contractor problems are additional services; track them so they can be billed.
Near completion, walk the site with the contractor and client to build the punch list, and return to check it is done before hand-over.
